title: Genetics
description: How traits pass from parents to children: Mendel's laws, Punnett squares, and inheritance beyond simple dominance.
objectives: Use the vocabulary of inheritance correctly
Solve monohybrid crosses including sex-linked traits
Explain incomplete dominance, codominance and blood groups

topics.title: Mendel and Inheritance
topics.description: Genes, alleles and genotypes; Mendel's pea experiments and the 3:1 ratio.

lessons.title: Genes, Alleles and Genotypes
lessons.description: The vocabulary of inheritance and how Mendel discovered its rules.
objectives: Define gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous
Explain Mendel's method and why peas were ideal
State the 3:1 phenotypic ratio and what it proves
lessons.introduction: Why do you resemble your parents but match neither exactly? In a monastery garden in the 1860s, Gregor Mendel grew 29,000 pea plants and found the mathematical rules behind the answer.

contents.title: The vocabulary
contents.body: A GENE is a DNA section coding for one trait (e.g. seed shape). An ALLELE is one version of a gene (round R vs wrinkled r). GENOTYPE is the allele pair an organism carries (RR, Rr, rr); PHENOTYPE is the observable trait (round or wrinkled). DOMINANT alleles show in heterozygotes (Rr looks round); RECESSIVE alleles show only when homozygous (rr). HOMOZYGOUS = identical alleles (RR or rr); HETEROZYGOUS = different alleles (Rr). CARRIERS (e.g. HbAHbS) carry a recessive allele without showing it. Mendel's genius was METHOD: he used pure-breeding lines, crossed them, counted THOUSANDS of offspring, and tracked ONE trait at a time. Peas were perfect: fast-growing, self- or cross-pollinating, with sharply contrasting traits (tall/short, round/wrinkled, green/yellow).

contents.title: The 3:1 ratio
contents.body: Cross pure tall (TT) with pure short (tt): all F1 offspring are Tt (all tall — dominance hides t). Self-cross the F1 (Tt × Tt): the F2 generation averages 3 tall : 1 short. Mendel's explanation — the LAW OF SEGREGATION: allele pairs separate into different gametes during meiosis, so each gamete carries ONE allele, and pairs reunite randomly at fertilisation. The wrinkled trait never blended away — it was CARRIED invisibly and reappeared. This disproved blending inheritance and founded genetics. His second law — INDEPENDENT ASSORTMENT: different gene pairs assort independently (Module 4's metaphase I lottery) — holds for genes on different chromosomes.

contents.title: Worked example: the F2 ratio
contents.body: Question: In tomatoes, red fruit (R) is dominant over yellow (r). Two heterozygous red plants are crossed. Predict the offspring ratio. Step 1 — Parent genotypes: Rr × Rr. Step 2 — Gametes: each parent makes R and r (segregation). Step 3 — Punnett square: rows R, r × columns R, r gives RR, Rr, Rr, rr. Step 4 — Phenotypes: 3 red : 1 yellow; genotypes 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr. Examination format: ALWAYS show parents, gametes, square, then genotype AND phenotype ratios — each line earns marks. Use the correct case convention (dominant capital, recessive lowercase of the SAME letter).

contents.title: Watch: Alleles and Genes
contents.body: Watch 'Alleles and Genes' by the Amoeba Sisters (official channel stream). Pause and define all eight vocabulary terms from memory before continuing.

contents.title: Key concepts
contents.body:
Gene = trait unit; allele = version; genotype = pair carried; phenotype = trait seen.
Dominant shows in heterozygotes; recessive needs homozygosity.
Segregation: alleles part into gametes. Independent assortment: pairs assort freely.
Tt × Tt gives 3:1 phenotypes, 1:2:1 genotypes.

contents.title: Lesson summary
contents.body: Mendel counted peas and discovered that inheritance comes in discrete units that segregate and reassort. Eight vocabulary terms and the 3:1 ratio are the keys to every genetics calculation ahead.

lessons.title: Solving Monohybrid Crosses
lessons.description: A five-step method for every single-trait cross, including test crosses and pedigrees.
objectives: Apply the five-step cross method to any monohybrid problem
Use test crosses to reveal unknown genotypes
Read simple pedigrees for dominant and recessive traits
lessons.introduction: Genetics problems look frightening until you learn the method. With five disciplined steps, every monohybrid cross — in homework, WAEC or JAMB — surrenders.

contents.title: The five-step method
contents.body: STEP 1 — SYMBOLS: assign letters (dominant capital: A; recessive lowercase: a) and state what each means. STEP 2 — PARENTS: write both genotypes with phenotypes (e.g. Aa tall × aa short). STEP 3 — GAMETES: list each parent's possible gametes (Aa makes A and a; aa makes only a). STEP 4 — SQUARE: draw the Punnett grid, fill every box. STEP 5 — RATIOS: state genotype ratio AND phenotype ratio (or probabilities). TEST CROSS: to reveal an unknown dominant phenotype (A? ), cross with homozygous recessive (aa) — if ANY recessive offspring appear, the parent was heterozygous; if dozens of offspring are all dominant, it is almost certainly AA. PEDIGREES: dominant traits appear every generation (affected children always have an affected parent); recessive traits skip generations and appear from carrier parents; if two normal parents have an affected child, the trait MUST be recessive.

contents.title: Worked example: the mystery bull
contents.body: Question: In cattle, hornless (H) is dominant over horned (h). A hornless bull is mated with horned cows (hh) and produces 12 calves — 6 hornless, 6 horned. What is the bull's genotype? Step 1 — Symbols: H hornless, h horned. Step 2 — Parents: bull H? × hh cows. Step 3 — Reason: horned calves (hh) must get h from EACH parent, so the bull carries h → the bull is Hh. Step 4 — Check: Hh × hh predicts 1:1, matching the observed 6:6. Step 5 — Conclude: heterozygous (Hh), proven by a test cross. Notice: the RECESSIVE offspring revealed the hidden allele — this logic cracks every 'find the genotype' question.

contents.title: Worked example: pedigree reading
contents.body: Question: A pedigree shows normal parents with one affected son and one normal daughter. Is the trait dominant or recessive? Step 1 — Test dominant: a dominant trait needs an affected parent to pass the allele — but BOTH parents are normal, so dominant is IMPOSSIBLE. Step 2 — Test recessive: two carrier parents (Aa × Aa) can produce aa children — possible. Step 3 — Conclude: recessive; both parents are carriers, the son is aa, the daughter is AA or Aa. Golden rule: normal parents + affected child = RECESSIVE, always. (Affected parent + normal children in every generation suggests dominant.)

contents.title: Key concepts
contents.body:
Five steps: symbols → parents → gametes → square → ratios.
Test cross: unknown dominant × homozygous recessive reveals the genotype.
Normal parents + affected child = recessive trait.
Recessive offspring prove a parent carried the hidden allele.

contents.title: Lesson summary
contents.body: Monohybrid crosses yield to method: symbols, parents, gametes, square, ratios. Test crosses expose hidden alleles, and pedigrees reveal dominance patterns — normal parents with an affected child always means recessive.

key_points: Test crosses use homozygous recessive partners

topics.title: Beyond Simple Dominance
topics.description: Incomplete dominance, codominance, blood groups and sex-linked inheritance.

lessons.title: Incomplete Dominance and Blood Groups
lessons.description: When heterozygotes blend or show both alleles — snapdragons, sickle cell and ABO.
objectives: Explain ABO blood groups as multiple alleles + codominance
Predict safe blood transfusions from donor and recipient groups
lessons.introduction: Red snapdragon × white snapdragon gives... pink. Neither allele dominates — Mendel's rules still apply, but dominance itself has shades.

contents.title: Three dominance patterns
contents.body: COMPLETE DOMINANCE: heterozygote matches one parent (Tt peas are tall). INCOMPLETE DOMINANCE: heterozygote is INTERMEDIATE — red snapdragon (CRCR) × white (CWCW) gives all pink (CRCW); self-crossing pinks gives 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white (note: use SUPERSCRIPT letters, never Rr, to avoid implying dominance). CODOMINANCE: heterozygote shows BOTH traits fully — roan cattle (red + white hairs), and human AB blood (both A and B antigens). MULTIPLE ALLELES: more than two alleles exist in the population — ABO blood has THREE (IA, IB, i): IA and IB are codominant with each other, both dominant over i. Genotypes: group A = IAIA or IAi; B = IBIB or IBi; AB = IAIB; O = ii (universal donor — no antigens; AB is universal recipient — no antibodies).

contents.title: Sickle cell: dominance depends on the level
contents.body: Sickle-cell anaemia shows dominance beautifully: at the MOLECULAR level, HbAHbS carriers make both normal and sickle haemoglobin (codominance); at the ORGANISM level in normal air, carriers look healthy (recessive disease); under severe oxygen shortage, carriers can show symptoms (incomplete dominance). One gene, three answers — dominance describes RELATIONSHIPS, not alleles alone. In malaria regions, carriers survive best (heterozygote advantage — the final-exam favourite), keeping the HbS allele common despite the disease. Genetic counselling lets carrier couples understand their 1-in-4 risk per pregnancy.

contents.title: Worked example: blood-group cross
contents.body: Question: A group-A mother (genotype IAi) and group-B father (IBi) have children. What blood groups are possible? Step 1 — Gametes: mother IA or i; father IB or i. Step 2 — Square: IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B), ii (O). Step 3 — Conclude: ALL FOUR groups possible — A, B, AB and O, each 1/4. Transfusion rule to memorise: give red cells lacking antigens the recipient's antibodies attack — O donates to all (no antigens); AB receives from all (no antibodies). Rh factor adds a second check in real medicine.

contents.title: Key concepts
contents.body:
Incomplete = blended heterozygote (pink snapdragons, 1:2:1). Codominant = both shown (roan, AB blood).
ABO: IA, IB codominant; both beat i. O = universal donor; AB = universal recipient.
Sickle cell shows all three dominance patterns at different levels.

contents.title: Lesson summary
contents.body: Dominance is a relationship, not a property: alleles can dominate, blend or share. ABO blood groups combine multiple alleles with codominance, and sickle cell proves that the same gene can show every pattern at once.

lessons.title: Sex-Linked Inheritance
lessons.description: Why haemophilia and colour blindness mostly affect males — genes on the X chromosome.
objectives: Explain why X-linked recessive traits hit males harder
lessons.introduction: Queen Victoria's descendants carried haemophilia across Europe's royal families — through daughters who never bled, to sons who did. The X chromosome explains it all.

contents.title: X-linked recessive logic
contents.body: Females are XX, males XY. The X carries 1000+ genes (including blood-clotting factor VIII and colour-vision genes); the tiny Y carries few, mostly male-determining. An X-linked RECESSIVE allele (Xh) shows in females only when homozygous (XhXh) but in males with a SINGLE copy (XhY) — males have no second X to mask it. Hence: males affected far more often; affected fathers pass Xh to ALL daughters (making them carriers) but NEVER to sons (sons get Y from father); carrier mothers pass to HALF their sons (affected) and half their daughters (carriers). Colour blindness (red-green) follows identical logic and is the commonest example (~8% of males). Notation: always write XHXH, XHXh, XhXh, XHY, XhY — bare 'Hh' loses marks in sex-linked questions.

contents.title: Worked example: the carrier mother
contents.body: Question: A normal-vision woman whose father was colour-blind marries a normal-vision man. What proportion of their sons will be colour-blind? Step 1 — Deduce her genotype: her father (XhY) gave her his ONLY X (Xh), so she is XHXh (carrier) — her normal vision proves the XH. Step 2 — Cross: XHXh × XHY. Step 3 — Sons: get Y from father, XH or Xh from mother → HALF the sons (XhY) colour-blind. Step 4 — Note daughters: all get XH from father, so all see normally (half carriers). Examination trap: 'father to son' transmission of X-linked traits is IMPOSSIBLE — any pedigree showing it rules out X-linkage.

contents.title: Watch: Mega Genetics Review
contents.body: Watch 'Mega Genetics Review: Mendelian and non-Mendelian Genetics' by the Amoeba Sisters (official channel stream) — it revises this whole module with practice problems. Attempt each problem before the solution appears.

contents.title: Key concepts
contents.body:
X-linked recessive: females need two copies; males need one — males affected more.
Fathers give X to daughters only; mothers give X to both.
Always use XHXh/XHY notation for sex-linked crosses.
Father-to-son transmission rules OUT X-linkage.

contents.title: Lesson summary
contents.body: The X chromosome's gene load, plus males' single copy, makes X-linked recessive traits a male-heavy pattern. Carrier mothers and affected fathers transmit predictably — trace the X's to solve any pedigree.

practical.title: Traits in Your Community Survey
practical.objective: Collect real inheritance data on observable traits and test whether ratios match genetic predictions.
practical.scenario: You are a field geneticist surveying at least 30 people (family, friends, classmates).
practical.instructions: 1. Survey 30+ people for THREE traits: tongue rolling (roller/non-roller), earlobe attachment (free/attached), and right/left thumb dominance when clasping hands. 2. Record counts in a table and convert to percentages. 3. For tongue rolling (modelled as dominant R): use the Hardy-Weinberg idea qualitatively — if 75% roll, what does that suggest about allele frequencies? (No calculation required — just argue whether R looks common or rare.) 4. Interview one family: record a trait across two generations and draw a mini-pedigree. 5. Write a conclusion: do your ratios resemble 3:1? Why might small samples deviate? SAFETY & ETHICS: participation voluntary; no names recorded (Person 1, 2...); no tasting of any test papers (some schools use PTC — do NOT use chemicals without teacher supervision).
practical.expected_output: Count tables with percentages, one mini-pedigree, and a 5-sentence conclusion on ratios and sample size.
evaluation_criteria: At least 30 people surveyed across 3 traits with honest counts
Conclusion links deviations to sample size and real-world complexity

assignment.title: Genetics Problem Clinic
assignment.description: Solve six structured genetics problems and explain one inheritance story in plain language.
assignment.instructions: Solve ALL six with full five-step working (symbols, parents, gametes, square, ratios): 1. Tall (T) × short (tt), all offspring tall — deduce the tall parent's genotype. 2. Black coat (B) dominant in goats: Bb × Bb — ratios? 3. Pink snapdragons self-crossed — offspring phenotypes? 4. Group O mother × group AB father — possible children groups? 5. Carrier haemophilia mother (XHXh) × normal father — probability of affected daughter? 6. Normal parents, colour-blind son — explain with genotypes. Then write 150–200 words explaining to a friend why two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child (recessive alleles, carriers).
assignment.requirements: Full working for every problem; answers alone earn half marks.
assignment.expected_output: Six fully worked crosses + plain-language explanation paragraph.
evaluation_criteria: Correct genotypes/ratios with complete five-step working
Explanation uses carrier logic accurately in simple words

quiz.title: Module 5 Quiz — Genetics
quiz.description: Quick check on vocabulary, monohybrid crosses and sex linkage.

questions.question: An organism with genotype Tt is best described as:
questions.explanation: Tt carries two DIFFERENT alleles — the definition of heterozygous. (Hemizygous describes X-linked genes in males.)

questions.question: Tt × Tt is expected to produce:
questions.explanation: The Punnett square gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt — three tall phenotypes to one short (genotypes 1:2:1).

questions.question: Pink snapdragons crossed together give red, pink and white offspring. This shows:
questions.explanation: The heterozygote is intermediate (pink) and the cross gives 1:2:1 — classic incomplete dominance.

questions.question: A group AB person has genotype:
questions.explanation: AB expresses both codominant alleles IA and IB. (IAi is group A, IBi is group B, ii is group O.)

questions.question: X-linked recessive traits affect more males because:
options: Males need only one copy on their single X to show the trait
The Y chromosome destroys dominant alleles
questions.explanation: Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes — one Xh with no masking second copy means the trait shows.

assessment.title: Module 5 Examination — Genetics
assessment.description: End-of-module examination covering Mendel, crosses, blood groups and sex linkage.
assessment.instructions: Answer ALL 6 questions in 25 minutes. Pass mark is 60%. Counts toward your final assessment gate.

questions.question: In guinea pigs, rough coat (R) is dominant over smooth (r). A rough × smooth cross gives 50% rough, 50% smooth offspring. The rough parent's genotype is:
questions.explanation: Smooth (rr) offspring must receive r from the rough parent, so it is Rr — a test-cross pattern giving 1:1.

questions.question: Two normal parents have an albino child. The most likely explanation is:
options: Both parents are carriers of a recessive allele
questions.explanation: Normal parents + affected child proves recessive inheritance: both parents are Aa carriers (each pregnancy carries 1/4 risk).

questions.question: A group O mother and group A father (genotype IAIA) can have children of group:
questions.explanation: Father gives IA to every child, mother gives i: all children IAi = group A. (An IAi father could also give O children.)

questions.question: A colour-blind man (XhY) and a normal homozygous woman (XHXH) have daughters who are:
options: All normal vision but all carriers
questions.explanation: Daughters get Xh from father and XH from mother: all XHXh — normal vision, obligate carriers.

questions.question: True or False: A father can pass an X-linked gene directly to his son.
questions.explanation: False. Sons receive Y (not X) from their father; their X comes from their mother. Father-to-son transmission rules out X-linkage.

questions.question: Which crosses can produce a group O child? (Select ALL that apply)
questions.explanation: O children (ii) need an i from each parent: IAi × IBi can give ii, and O × O always gives ii. AB × O gives only A/B children; IAIA × IBIB gives only AB.
